prize_parts.citation: For discoveries in the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and the incretin effect, and for their translation into long-acting incretin therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: After reading the full first round, I keep B041 with Drucker, Holst and Knudsen. The scientific case is the complete chain: the incretin effect and proglucagon biology, the identification of GLP-1 as the insulinotropic hormone in humans, the problem of rapid degradation, and long-acting agonists whose benefit in diabetes, obesity, and cardiovascular and renal outcomes has been confirmed in independent randomized trials. The result is mature and the clinical consequence is established, not projected. The decisive point for me is that the discovery changed medicine only when a stable molecule could be given to patients, so the protraction step belongs in the citation. The citation is worded around physiology and its translation so that three names describe it without overstating any one contribution. Unanimity in the openings is not my argument. The chain itself is.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is still credit. The committee is split three to three on the third name, and Mojsov's characterization of the active GLP-1(7-36) form is a real contribution. Her priority relative to the Habener group cannot be settled from the supplied record, and Habener is not on the credited list. My configuration also joins two physiologists with an industrial drug developer, which can be read as merging a discovery and a product. If the committee decides that only the discovery strand is prize-worthy, Drucker, Holst and Mojsov is the cleaner basic-science trio and I would not regard it as unreasonable. I hold my choice with moderate confidence, because it depends on a judgement about what the prize should reward and not on a documented fact.

responses.point: Linnarsson argues that identifying the active GLP-1(7-36) form is part of the discovery itself, whereas acylation and half-life extension are engineering built on a known action. He also names Drucker, Holst and Knudsen as his fallback.
responses.response: I accept that the distinction is real, and your willingness to fall back on the Knudsen trio makes the gap between us smaller than the three-to-three split suggests. I still weigh it differently. A known action of a peptide with a half-life of minutes was not a medicine. Choosing a chemical route to protraction, and showing in patients that it works, was a creative step and not routine optimisation. I would be more persuaded by Mojsov if the record showed that the active form was identified independently of the Habener group and was a necessary precondition for the drug design. Our text does not show that. Since I cannot judge it from the supplied material, I do not think a contested priority claim should displace a contribution whose role is not contested.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius would accept Knudsen over Mojsov only if the committee decides the prize is for the therapy rather than the discovery, and asks that the Mojsov documentation be examined first. She also keeps B004 as her second alternative.
responses.response: That is a fair framing, and it is where I think the committee must be explicit. My view is that the prize is for a discovery that changed a field, and in this case the field changed through the full chain, which includes the long-acting agonist. I do not think that places the therapy above the discovery, because Holst and Drucker still carry the physiology in the citation. I agree the Mojsov documentation should be examined, and I would move if it showed her contribution was decisive and independent. On B004, your arguments on attribution and on 20 years of survival data have moved me. I now give B004 as my second alternative in place of B033, because B033 has six credited names for three places and B004 has the cleanest credit on the list. I still rank B035 first among alternatives because CAR-T opened a new modality, but I would not resist B004 if the committee wants a configuration with minimal attribution dispute.

responses.point: Sandberg keeps Mojsov third because the prize tradition rewards the discovery that made development rational. She asks that the committee state whether Mojsov's inclusion rests on peptide chemistry and characterization and not on first discovery of the hormone.
responses.response: I agree with your request, and it applies to both options. If Mojsov were chosen, the citation would have to say that her credit is for characterization of the active peptide, since the first discovery of the hormone belongs to others. If Knudsen is chosen, the citation must say that her credit is for the design of protracted analogues. You also say a two-part prize cannot fit within three people without dropping someone, and I agree. That is why I keep a single achievement and a citation that covers physiology and translation, instead of presenting two linked parts. I disagree that the drug-design step is a second achievement outside the discovery. In this case I read it as the step that completed the achievement.

responses.point: Svenningsson, as chair, keeps Knudsen in the trio but says the configuration should be reconsidered if the committee decides the basic and drug-design strands deserve separate recognition. He asks whether B041 is simply the most obvious name on the list.
responses.response: I share that check and I tried to apply it. The obviousness concern would worry me if the support rested on reputation. Here it rests on independently confirmed outcome data, and I cannot find a candidate on the shortlist with a more complete chain from mechanism to clinical consequence. On separate recognition, I do not see enough room: a two-part prize would need three names for the incretin strand and another achievement with its own names, and the limit of three people overall would force us to drop either Holst or Drucker, or give the second part only one name. I do not favour that. I therefore keep the single-part configuration, and I agree the choice of a third name should be argued openly and not covered by the vote count.

responses.point: Perlmann holds optogenetics as a second alternative but says the attribution problem is a serious obstacle, and says he would reconsider the third name if Mojsov's contribution were shown to be decisive and independent of Habener's.
responses.response: I agree with both points. Your analysis of the attribution of B033 is what changed my alternatives. Among six credited names for three places, Bamberg, Boyden and Miesenboeck each have claims, so any trio would be contestable. Although optogenetics is close to my own field, I cannot see how to defend a three-name split, and its clinical translation remains early. I therefore no longer list B033 among my alternatives and move B004 in its place. On Mojsov we share the same condition: the decision turns on documentary evidence that we do not have in the supplied text. Until it is shown, I cannot treat the priority claim as established.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's characterization of the active GLP-1(7-36) form was independent of and decisive relative to the Habener group's work cannot be settled from the supplied text, and this is the factor that could change my third name.
Whether one citation can describe both the physiology and the long-acting drug development with three names without misrepresenting either contribution.
Whether Knudsen's protraction chemistry was a creative invention or a refinement of existing approaches depends on a reading of the development record that I have not verified.
Whether the credited list for B035 is complete without Eshhar, and whether B004 should rank above it as an alternative on attribution grounds.
I am relying on recollection of the literature and have not verified details against primary sources.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with any shortlisted candidate is apparent from my profile. I co-authored a 2009 paper with committee colleague Thomas Perlmann and a 2019 synthesis with Sten Grillner, and neither relates to the shortlisted discoveries. Optogenetics (B033) is in my general field of neuroscience, but I have no documented involvement with its credited names, and I no longer list it among my alternatives. My disclosure is otherwise unchanged from round 1.
